🧭 Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar

Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis
Central or eccentric low-signal/low-attenuation regions in hepatic masses must first be classified as true scar versus necrosis, hemorrhage, fat, fibrosis, or treated tumor. The highest-yield separation uses scar signal/calcification, enhancement kinetics, multiplicity, and associated vascular, biliary, or capsular findings.

🔍 Key Imaging Findings
  • FNH: homogeneous arterial hyperenhancement; later becomes similar to liver; central scar is T2 bright, can enhance late with extracellular contrast, and does not retain gadoxetate.
  • Giant hemangioma: peripheral discontinuous nodular blood-pool enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in; very T2 bright; fibrotic central scar may remain nonenhancing and may calcify.
  • Conventional HCC: heterogeneous hypervascular mass, often with washout; mosaic architecture/necrosis can mimic scar; venous invasion strongly supports HCC.
  • Hepatic adenoma: apparent scar-like regions often represent hemorrhage, necrosis, fibrosis, or fat; chemical-shift signal loss can reveal intracellular lipid.
  • Metastases: central low density usually represents necrosis or fibrosis; mucinous metastases can calcify; most metastases are best seen on portal venous phase.
  • Fibrolamellar HCC: large heterogeneous mass in a young noncirrhotic patient with a classic fibrotic central scar; the scar is T1/T2 dark in Core and commonly calcified in the article package.
  • Mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma: delayed/progressive enhancement from fibrous stroma; capsular retraction and biliary/portal obstruction support the diagnosis.
  • Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma: multiple peripheral/subcapsular nodules that may coalesce, often with target appearance and capsular retraction.
  • Large regenerative nodules/NRH in Budd-Chiari: often multiple hypervascular nodules with central scars; delayed hepatobiliary-agent retention supports functional hepatocytes.
⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Common: FNH; cavernous hemangioma.
  • Less common: conventional HCC; adenoma; metastases; fibrolamellar HCC; cholangiocarcinoma; epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.
  • Rare but important: large regenerative nodules / nodular regenerative hyperplasia in Budd-Chiari syndrome.
⚠️ Pearls / Pitfalls
  • Calcified scar strongly favors fibrolamellar HCC or giant hemangioma, but mucinous metastases can also calcify.
  • Do not call every central low-attenuation focus a scar: adenoma, metastases, and HCC commonly contain necrosis/hemorrhage/fibrosis instead.
  • FNH versus fibrolamellar HCC: FNH scar is T2 bright and enhances late with extracellular agents; fibrolamellar scar is fibrotic and T1/T2 dark.
  • Portal or hepatic venous invasion is a major discriminator favoring HCC over cholangiocarcinoma or metastases.
⭐ Super Summary
Scar composition + enhancement kinetics + calcification + multiplicity + vascular/biliary/capsular behavior is the practical workstation algorithm.

column11: Why does FNH retain hepatobiliary contrast while its central scar does not?
column12: FNH contains functioning hepatocytes and biliary ductules, so the lesion takes up and retains hepatobiliary contrast and is typically iso- to hyperintense to liver on the hepatobiliary phase. The central scar is composed of biliary ductules and venules but does not behave like functioning hepatocyte-rich parenchyma, so it does not retain gadoxetate. With extracellular contrast, the scar may enhance late. Radiologic pivot: lesion uptake with scar nonretention strongly supports FNH over adenoma.

Radiologic pivot: functional biliary/Kupffer-cell behavior can support FNH over adenoma.
